title: Dates and Shelf Life — Shift Leader Walk
description:
This walk is about dates. It is one of the six biggest food safety risks the brand tracks.

Start at the make table. Then finish it standing in your walk-in with the door open. Nothing here is a memory test. The dates are right in front of you. Read them.

questions.title: Today is Monday, November 16. Tap each product to see its date. Then tap the one that should already be gone.

hotspots.label: The bacon. Its date was Sunday, and today is Monday.
hotspots.why: It should have been thrown out last night at close.

questions.help: This is our own make table. Our labels say Made, Ready, and Discard.
questions.explanation:
The bacon. Its label says Sunday 11/15. Today is Monday.

• The Italian sausage says Monday 11/16. That is today, so it is still fine. It goes tonight at close.
• The pepperoni and the ham are both still days away.
• Only the bacon is late, and only by one night.

This is the one that catches stores out. Nobody threw it out at close. It was still there in the morning. Now it costs us points.

Throw out dated food at close. Not in the morning.

questions.title: The company that made these diced tomatoes printed a date on the bag. Today is one day after that date. How does the auditor score it?
choices: It does not count. One day is close enough.
Secondary — the less serious kind
Significant — the most serious kind
It does not count, because the bag is still sealed.
questions.explanation:
Significant. This is the most serious kind.

• There is no grace day. One day late is late.
• A Significant problem has to be fixed within 24 hours.
• A sealed bag does not help. Sealed and out of date is still out of date.

This really happened to us. An auditor found diced tomatoes in one of our walk-ins. The date said June 13. He found them June 14. One day. It scored Significant.

questions.title: We opened a tub of Alfredo and wrote our own date on it. Today is two days after the date we wrote. How does the auditor score it?
choices: Significant — the same as the tomatoes
Secondary — the less serious kind
It does not count. We wrote the date, so we can change it.
It does not count, because the company did not print that date.
questions.explanation:
Secondary. Whose date it is changes how much it hurts.

• The company's date, past — Significant.
• Our own date, past — Secondary.
• Something we opened with no date at all — also Secondary.

Both of these came off the same cooler on the same day. The tomatoes scored Significant. The Alfredo scored Secondary.

The Secondary one is the one we control. A marker fixes it.

questions.title: A bag has two dates on it: "Sell By 11/20" and "Best By 11/28". Which one do we go by?
choices: Best By 11/28, because it is later
Sell By 11/20, because it is earlier
Neither. Only a date that says "Expiration" counts.
Whichever one the company says is the real one
questions.explanation:
Always the earliest date on the bag.

• It does not matter what it is called. Best By, Use By, Sell By, Expiration — they all count.
• The earliest one wins. This bag is out of date after 11/20.

Looking for the latest date is how food sits in the cooler looking fine for another week.

questions.title: Which of these would cost us points? Pick all that apply.
choices: A sealed bag of cold food with no date printed on it anywhere
An opened bag of sauce with no date written on it
A tub we made three days ago, labeled, still good
A sealed case that is past the date on the box
An opened tub that is past the date we wrote on it
questions.explanation:
Four of these five cost us points.

• No date printed on it at all — Significant. A missing date counts as much as a late one.
• Opened, with no date written on it — Secondary.
• Sealed but past the date — Significant.
• Past the date we wrote — Secondary.

The tub we made three days ago is the only right one. It is labeled and still good. Somebody spent ten seconds with a marker, and that is all it took.

questions.title: You open a bag of ready-to-eat food and put it in the walk-in. You will keep it longer than one day. What has to happen?
choices: Nothing. The date on the bag still covers it.
Write a date on it. Use it or throw it out within 7 days.
Write a date on it. Use it or throw it out within 14 days.
Use it by the end of tomorrow.
questions.explanation:
Put a date on it. Then use it or throw it out within 7 days.

• Opening it starts a new clock. The date on the bag is no longer the only one.
• 7 days is the longest it can ever go. It is not a target.

Plenty of food is shorter than 7 days. Look at our own make table. The buttery sauce is made Wednesday and thrown out Thursday. That is one day.

Check Pizzapedia for the item in your hand. Do not give everything 7 days.

questions.title: It is 4pm. You find food with today's date on it. What do you do?
choices: Throw it out right now. It is already bad.
Keep using it today. Throw it out at close tonight.
Keep it until this time tomorrow.
Mark it down and use it first.
questions.explanation:
Use it today. Throw it out at close.

• The date on the label is the last day you can use it. It is not the first day it is bad.
• That is why our labels say Close. "Discard Thu 10/22 Close" means it goes at close on Thursday.

Throwing it out at 4pm wastes food. Leaving it for tomorrow costs us points. The label already tells you when. Somebody just has to do it.

questions.title: You found food that is past its date. What do you do? Pick all that apply.
choices: Take it off the shelf now, not at the end of your shift
Tell your manager
Check the rest of that food, and whatever is next to it
Use it today and order more for tomorrow
Find out why it got missed
questions.explanation:
Take it out, say something, check around it, and find out how it got there.

• Take it out now. "At the end of my shift" is how somebody else uses it without knowing.
• Check what is next to it. People skip this step, and it is the one that pays off. One bad item is almost never one bad item. Usually a delivery got put away in front of the older stock.
• Ask why. If nobody ever rotates that shelf, you just found next week's problem too.

Food that is past its date gets thrown out. You do not use it up because it is only a little late.

questions.title: Put these in order, from the box arriving to the food going out.
steps: Check the date on the box before you open it
Fill in the label: made, ready, and discard
Put it behind the older stock, not in front of it
Check it on your daily walk-in check
Throw it out at close on the discard date
questions.explanation:
Two steps get skipped: the fourth one and the last one.

• Check the date before you open it. That stops you putting a 7-day label on something that goes bad in two.
• Put it behind the older stock. That is all rotation is. Put it in front and the old food disappears from view, and it will still be there in three weeks.
• Throw it out at close. Skip this and it becomes a morning problem.

None of this takes extra time. It just has to happen in this order.

questions.title: PHOTO: Go in your walk-in. Find the food closest to its date, or already past it. Take a picture of the label so we can read the date.
questions.help: Find the closest one, not a tidy one. If something is already past its date, that is the picture we want. Circle the date.

questions.title: PHOTO: Find something WE opened and dated ourselves. Take a picture of our label on it.
questions.help: If you cannot find one opened item with our own date on it, take a picture of an opened item with no date. That tells us something too.

questions.title: How many items did you have to throw out or re-label on this walk?
questions.help: Zero is a real answer. So is eleven. Your Area Coach would rather have the true number.

questions.title: What are you going to change so this does not happen again? Say who will do it and when.
questions.help: Be specific. "Check dates daily" is not a plan. Who throws out dated food at close? Which shift checks the walk-in on the way in?
